problem: Whole-body mobile manipulation RL has a huge action space and a composite multi-objective reward. Prior work either hand-partitions actions into base and arm and manually assigns them to sub-objectives, which forfeits whole-body coordination, or applies vanilla RL, which struggles with high gradient variance.
motivation: Each reward term (e.g. base collision, end-effector orientation) is causally affected by only a subset of action dimensions, so the other dimensions contribute only noise to its gradient. Exploiting this structure can cut policy-gradient variance without hardcoded domain knowledge and without giving up simultaneous whole-body control.
key_idea: Automatically discover a binary action-dimension-to-reward-term causal matrix via conditional mutual information on random exploration data, then use it in a factored (causal) PPO policy gradient that aggregates advantages only from causally related reward terms.
insight: The fine-grained discovered causal matrix matters. In iGibson, a hand-coded arm-base factorization gives no gain over vanilla PPO (76.1/78.7 vs 74.3/79.0 success), while the discovered matrix reaches 93.6/92.1. In Minigrid, a random factorization fails completely and does worse than vanilla PPO, and an over-specified one is only slightly worse than the exact discovered matrix. The gain is larger on HSR, whose discovered matrix is sparser than Fetch's, consistent with the variance-reduction explanation.
method: Action-reward causal discovery: collect (s,a,r) tuples with a random policy, which makes action dimensions uncorrelated (assumption A3). Estimate CMI(a_i, r_j) and threshold it (epsilon=0.02, k=1) to fill the n x m binary causal matrix B.

CMI estimator: per reward channel j, a network maps each action dimension and the state to 128-d features, takes an element-wise max, and predicts r_j through a head. Masking one action feature to -inf gives the conditional without a_i, so only m models are needed instead of n x m; training maximizes the log-likelihood of both terms.

Theory: Theorem 1 says that under A1-A4 (causal Markov, faithfulness, uncorrelated exploration actions, short-horizon dependence), a_i->r_j iff a_i is conditionally dependent on r_j given the other actions and the state. Theorem 2 says the gradient is unbiased if B is correct.

Causal policy gradient: grad = grad log pi(a|s) . B . A_vec, where the policy is factored per action dimension and A_vec is the per-reward-term advantage. It is a special case of Factored Policy Gradient (Spooner et al.) with the causal graph learned rather than given.

Causal PPO: the value network is multi-headed (one output per reward term) and GAE is computed per term. The per-action-dimension advantage is B.A, and the PPO clipped objective updates each action dimension with its own advantage.

Sim-to-real pipeline: train in iGibson on an 11-D action space with 8 reward terms (reach, eef orientation/height, base/arm/self collision, head orientation, gripper) using LiDAR and proprioception. Transfer zero-shot to Gazebo and a real Toyota HSR, with the goal tracked through a QR marker.

setting.backbone: MLP policy and value networks (PPO) with small CNN LiDAR encoder, trained from scratch; plus CMI causal-discovery network
setting.training_data: RL in simulation (Minigrid; iGibson with Fetch and HSR in 8 household scenes) with randomized goals and obstacles, plus a random-policy exploration dataset for causal discovery; no real-world training
setting.observation: 270-D (HSR) / 220-D (Fetch) LiDAR scan + proprioception and task vector (25-D HSR, 27-D Fetch: relative goal position, goal orientation); the goal is estimated via QR marker in the real world
setting.action_space: continuous 11-D whole-body: base velocity, 2D head pan/tilt, arm (HSR joint deltas, Fetch Cartesian eef deltas), gripper; Minigrid uses 4 discrete 3-valued dimensions
setting.privileged: none (only onboard sensors at test time; the CBiRRT2 baselines get the environment layout)

numbers_note: Not a navigation-benchmark paper; results are on custom mobile-manipulation tasks (iGibson reaching, Gazebo, real HSR), reported as success rates and none fit the canonical benchmark list. Key values are in results. The Minigrid and iGibson training curves appear only in figures.
results: In iGibson, Causal MoMa reaches 93.6% (HSR) and 92.1% (Fetch) success over 1000 trials, against vanilla PPO at 74.3%/79.0% and FPPO arm-base at 76.1%/78.7%. In Gazebo it scores 20/20, 20/20, 19/20 and 20/20 over four scenarios, while SLQ-MPC gets 20/20, 17/20, 3/20 and 9/20. On the real HSR (zero-shot, 9 runs each) it beats CBiRRT2 and CBiRRT2-replan in 5 of 6 scenarios (e.g. dynamic goal + dynamic obstacles 8/9 at d=0.15 m and 9/9 at d=0.3 m, versus 0/9 and 0/9 for CBiRRT2 and 0/9 and 2/9 for replan).
limitations: Assumption A4 (short-horizon causal dependence) fails with sparse, delayed rewards at k=1 (a larger k=5 recovers them in a toy case), and the method needs a factored reward.
The policy is reactive from partial LiDAR and cannot plan long detours around local minima (it failed in the sofa-bed static-obstacle case); a wrong or random causal matrix hurts training badly.
The policy does not consume raw images (the goal comes from a QR marker), and the tasks are limited to reaching-style skills.
builds_on: Causal dynamics model discovery (Wang et al. 2022)
